summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and, in 2020, became the first Central American country to adopt marriage equality. Its courts have extended that posture into concrete holdings: in 2000 the Supreme Court ordered a gay sauna to remain open, ruling that subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis and violate constitutional rights, and in 2011 the same court reversed its 2008 position to allow same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Name changes on official identity cards have been handled by the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones since May 2018 through a simple, free procedure. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

In 2020 the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate-crime penalties. Amending article 112 of the Penal Code, it set 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation; article 380 now carries 1 to 3 years for exclusion or segregation on that basis; and article 386bis provides 3 to 10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail motivated by sexual orientation. The published provisions are framed around sexual orientation, and the sources reviewed do not state that gender identity is named in them.

No visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travellers appears in current law. In December 2018 President Carlos Alvarado Quesada signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. The one documented instance of entry discrimination is historical: in 1990 the Minister of the Interior instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting. That directive is decades old and is not described as current.

Detention is the sharpest documented risk for a trans person. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, through Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation to the facility matching gender identity, strictly voluntary and decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module was under consideration, with Spain's system cited as the model alongside protocols developed with CEJIL since 2016. Two years later the policy was not holding. In June 2019 CRHoy reported that Stephanie, a trans woman serving roughly six years for complicity in drug trafficking, was held at the CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility where, she said, only men were held; she transitioned while incarcerated and described prison as offering only two options. The Justice Ministry told the outlet there were 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time. Stephanie recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick handle at La Reforma in Alajuela, witnessed by a custodian.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific protective legislation, while recording her concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection as a basis for policy and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

Rollback pressure is real and current. A conversion-therapy bill has been stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol. Conservative lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other parties called the presidential rainbow flag flown at the Casa Presidencial in May 2014 a 'provocation' while a same-sex civil union bill was pending, and the 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
Official recognition has been unusually visible for the region. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, with President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directing public institutions to facilitate, promote and support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May 2014; President Alvarado issued a public apology in 2018 to the LGBT community for past state persecution, citing state promoted and executed persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings, and became the first Costa Rican president to march at the San José pride parade in June 2019, an event drawing about 100,000 participants.

That recognition sits alongside sustained organised opposition and a social environment that has not caught up with the legal one. Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were formerly commonplace even while homosexuality was technically legal. Comprehensive sex education campaigns are described as almost nonexistent in Costa Rican public high schools because of opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups, and in 1993 a private university, Universidad Internacional de las Américas, was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff; the Ministry of Education said enforcing it would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33 and 70. A 2012 poll found 60% of 18 to 34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples, leaving substantial minority opposition.

The pace of change is uneven across adjacent areas. The Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that in-vitro fertilisation is unconstitutional, a ruling recorded in the partnership-benefits context, and a 2016 bill that would have allowed transgender people to change name and gender without surgery or judicial permission failed.
localsOnly:
Residents access gender marker and name changes through different routes. Since 2013 a transgender person can change legal name with a judicial order; since May 2018 name changes on official identity cards run through the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones by a simple, free procedure, and Executive Decree 41173-MP covers the gender marker without surgery or court involvement.

Partner recognition extends to social security. Survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans, announced by the Ministry of Labour on 25 June 2016, with an individual survivor benefit approved on 29 June 2018; the teachers' separate budget was excluded from the arrangement.

For prisoners, the Justice Ministry's 2017 circular established the voluntary placement choice and a census of self-identified trans inmates, with an exclusive module under consideration and case-by-case decisions made with prison social workers and psychologists. The 2019 reporting from CAI Orosi de Cartago indicates the choice was not consistently honoured in practice.

Education and youth policy shifted in 2025, when authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol, while a conversion-therapy bill has remained stalled since its 2019 committee report.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources reviewed state the 2020 hate-crime amendments in terms of sexual orientation and do not say whether article 112, article 380 or article 386bis also name gender identity or gender expression. Whether a trans visitor reporting a hate-motivated offence would be charged under those articles is therefore not established here.

Unresolved: no source documents how Costa Rican border or airport officials treat an entry document whose gender marker differs from the traveller's presentation. The absence of an LGBTQ-specific visa rule is sourced; screening practice in relation to gender markers is not.

Unresolved: the current status of the conversion-therapy bill after its 2019 committee report, and whether the 2025 withdrawal of the sex-education program and anti-bullying protocol affected trans-specific measures as distinct from broader LGB content, are not detailed in the inventory.

Not sourced: enforcement statistics for the 2020 hate-crime provisions, and any post-2019 update on the placement of the 23 transgender prisoners recorded in the national system. The ILGA World Database entry is listed as a reference for the country's LGBTI legal framework but its specific recorded values are not reproduced in the inventory.
